newsitem.title: USA: Key provisions of the 1997 U.S. budget accord.
newsitem.headline: Key provisions of the 1997 U.S. budget accord.

text.p: The White House and Congress Saturday put the final touches on the fiscal 1997 budget which authorizes $244 billion for the Pentagon and about $356 billion for domestic programs.

The bill funds agencies covered by six of the 13 annual spending bills Congress must approve. Seven have been acted on separately. It is expected to win final congressional approval Monday and be signed by President Clinton before the Oct. 1 start of the new fiscal year.
Among the provisions included in the omnibus appropriations bill are the following:

-- $500,000 to reimburse fired White House travel office chief Billy Dale and others in the office for legal expenses related to their defense against allegations of fraud and mishandling of accounts.
-- $2.9 billion expected to be raised from the sale of broadcast airwaves and $3.1 billion in added deposits to the thrift reserve fund. Banking regulatory changes.
-- A crackdown on illegal immigration that was shorn of many provisions critics said were mean-spirited towards legal immigrants.

-- $1.1 billion to fight terrorism with hiring of 300 more airport security personnel, more intelligence officers, a study of taggants in explosives other than black and smokeless powder, security improvements in U.S. embassies and federal offices. Clinton was not granted permission to increase the use of wiretaps in terrorism investigations.
-- $12.1 billion in foreign aid, of which $5.1 billion is for military and economic aid to Israel and Egypt and $19.6 million for Ireland.

-- Ties $385 million in U.S. aid to international family planning agencies to their agreement not to spend outside funds for abortion services. The money would not be released until July 1, 1997 unless Congress acts.

-- Reauthorization of the Overseas Private Investment Corp. (OPIC), a government program to back investors, and funds the International Development Association at $700 million, unchanged from last year, but $234 million less than Clinton requested.
-- $1.4 billion for Clinton's Community Oriented Policing designed to put 100,000 more police on the streets by 2000.
-- Provides that those convicted of child and spousal abuse would lose gun ownership rights.
-- $225 million for the joint government-industry research into advanced technology at the Commerce Department.
-- A three percent pay raise for the military.

-- Pell college student grants are raised to $2,700 a year, up $230 from 1996 and the highest level ever with funds for student loans at $41.6 billion, up $3.3 billion from 1996. Fully funds the college direct lending program.
-- $3.98 billion for Head Start preschools as requested by Clinton.
-- $1.1 billion for Job Corps, up $60 million from 1996 and $871 million for 550,000 youth summer jobs.
-- $650 million for fire fighting in Western states.
-- $400 million to help victims of Hurricane Fran.
-- $123 million for troop redeployment in Saudi Arabia.
-- $8.8 billion dedicated to the war on illegal drugs.
-- $1.3 billion as requested by Clinton for low income energy assistance.
-- $491 million for Goals 2000 elementary school improvements, up from $350 million as Clinton requested.
-- Health research at the National Institutes of Health increased to $12.7 billion, up $819 million from 1996.
-- Safe drinking water, pesticide and food safety laws fully funded.
-- Cuts the Internal Revenue Service funding $141 million to $7.2 billion.
